666.title: Divine Mercy Sunday
666.hook: the second Sunday of Easter, named by John Paul II in 2000
666.howItsDone: On Divine Mercy Sunday Catholic parishes often display the Divine Mercy image, hear the Gospel of doubting Thomas from John 20, offer confession, and pray the Divine Mercy chaplet, often at three in the afternoon; the words Jesus, I trust in you are printed beneath the image.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Easter octave: eight days kept as one. Your line was one long day. Today is the octave's last day.

In a convent in Poland in the 1930s, a young nun with little schooling kept a notebook. Her name was Faustina Kowalska. She wrote that Jesus had appeared to her, robed in white, with two rays streaming from his heart, one pale and one red. She was asked to have the image painted, with a short line of trust underneath. She died of tuberculosis in 1938, at thirty-three. Sixty-two years later, in Rome, a Polish pope declared her a saint, and gave a name to the Sunday that ends the Easter octave.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK IN A POLISH CONVENT.` → `TWO RAYS, PALE AND RED.` → `A LINE UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: On the thirtieth of April, 2000, John Paul II canonized Faustina and announced that, from then on, the second Sunday of Easter would be called Divine Mercy Sunday across the whole Church. The Latin word for mercy, misericordia, joins the heart, cor, to someone's misery. The readings didn't change. The Gospel this Sunday, in every year of the cycle, is John 20: the risen Jesus walking through locked doors, breathing on the disciples, and saying, in the Douay-Rheims, "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." He greets frightened friends who ran away with peace, shows them his wounds, and then hands them the power to forgive. Then Thomas, who wasn't there, gets his own visit a week later, and Jesus says: "Blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." The feast's theme was already in the text. Faustina's image puts it in a picture: in her diary, the two rays stand for the blood and water that flowed from his side. And the line at the bottom, in her Polish, is three words, Jezu, ufam Tobie. In English it's the line Catholics now pray: Jesus, I trust in you. A surprise: for about twenty years, the Vatican restricted this devotion, partly because of flawed copies of her writings. The restriction was lifted in 1978, the year a cardinal from Kraków, where she had lived, became pope. Catholics are free to take up Faustina's devotions or not; the Church approves them without requiring them. But the line itself is short enough for anyone to carry. In English, five words. Not I understand. Not I'm sure. Just trust.
screen: `NAMED ON 30 APRIL 2000.` · `THE GOSPEL: FORGIVE, AND THOMAS.` · `TWO RAYS: BLOOD AND WATER.` · `RESTRICTED, THEN LIFTED IN 1978.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HAVE NOT SEEN.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing settle and name one thing you're carrying that you can't fix today. If you pray, say Faustina's line on your breath, in on Jesus and out on the rest: Jesus, I trust in you. If you don't pray, simply hold the worry in an open hand instead of a fist.
misericordia. The Latin word for mercy, joining heart to someone's misery, behind the feast John Paul II named in 2000, when he canonized Saint Faustina. Today's word.
Your line: Jesus, I trust in you. It fits on a single breath. Until tomorrow.

667.title: Good Shepherd Sunday
667.hook: the fourth Sunday of Easter, a day of prayer for vocations
667.howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Easter Catholic parishes hear a Gospel from John 10 about the Good Shepherd and keep the World Day of Prayer for Vocations, praying for priests and religious, often with a talk from a seminarian or sister.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Divine Mercy Sunday and misericordia. Your line was Jesus, I trust in you.

Somebody calls your name across a crowded airport. You turn before you've even thought about it, not because the voice was loud, but because it was yours. Two Sundays after the octave ends, on the fourth Sunday of Easter, every Catholic parish in the world hears a Gospel about exactly that: a shepherd whose sheep know his voice. And since 1964 the Church has made it a day of prayer about a call.
screen: `A NAME ACROSS AN AIRPORT.` → `THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF EASTER.` → `A DAY ABOUT A CALL.`

segments.voice: Every year on this Sunday the Gospel comes from John chapter ten, a different slice of it in each year of the three-year cycle. In one year, the gate of the sheepfold, and this line, in the Douay-Rheims: "the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." In another, I am the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep. In the third, my sheep hear my voice, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand. A shepherd in Jesus's world didn't drive his flock from behind with dogs. He walked ahead and called, and they followed the voice they knew. The word vocation comes from the Latin vocare, to call. In 1964 Pope Paul VI began a World Day of Prayer for Vocations, and it settled on this Sunday. Most parishes pray especially for priests and for men and women entering religious life, and you'll often hear a seminarian or a sister speak at Mass. But the Church uses the word more widely than that. The Catechism speaks of a vocation to love that everyone has, and of marriage as a vocation too. A married couple, a single person caring for a parent, a nurse on night shifts: Catholic teaching says each of them can be answering a call. And the call in John isn't a job description first. It's a name. He calls his own by name, and then leads them out.
screen: `JOHN TEN, EVERY YEAR.` · `A SHEPHERD WALKS AHEAD AND CALLS.` · `VOCARE: TO CALL.` · `PRIESTS, SISTERS, MARRIAGE, EVERYONE.` · then, large: `HE CALLETH HIS OWN SHEEP BY NAME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you know who is at a fork right now: a young person wondering about the priesthood or the convent, a friend deciding whether to marry, change careers, or move home to care for someone. Picture their face and say their name quietly. If you pray, you can pray for them by name; if you don't, simply wish them clarity and courage.
Vocation. From the Latin vocare, to call. In Catholic teaching, a call from God, to priesthood, religious life, marriage, or a life of love in the world. Today's word.
Your line: he calls by name. Nobody is called as a number. Day six hundred sixty-seven, done.

668.title: Our Lady of Fatima (13 May)
668.hook: three shepherd children in Portugal in 1917, asking for prayer and penance
668.howItsDone: On 13 May Catholics often pray the rosary for peace, and pilgrims gather at the shrine in Fatima, Portugal, for candlelight processions; the appearances are approved as worthy of belief, but Catholics are not required to believe in them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Shepherd Sunday and vocation, a call that starts with a name. Your line was he calls by name.

May 1917. Europe is at war, and Portugal has sent its own soldiers to the trenches. In the hills near a village called Fatima, three children are watching sheep: Lucia, ten, and her younger cousins Francisco and Jacinta, eight and seven. Around noon on the thirteenth, they later said, a flash like lightning came, and then a lady brighter than the sun, standing over a small oak tree. She asked them to come back on the thirteenth of every month, and to pray the rosary every day, for peace in the world and the end of the war.
screen: `MAY 1917: EUROPE AT WAR.` → `THREE CHILDREN WITH SHEEP.` → `PRAY THE ROSARY FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: The children kept coming back, month after month through October. In August the local administrator held them, and that meeting came days late, away from the usual spot. The crowds grew from a handful of neighbors to thousands. On the thirteenth of October, in pouring rain, a huge crowd gathered, and witnesses, a reporter among them, described the sun seeming to spin and plunge. People still argue over what they saw. The message the children carried was simple and demanding: pray, especially the rosary; do penance; make sacrifices for sinners; pray for peace. Francisco and Jacinta took it so seriously that they offered up small hungers and discomforts, the way children would. Both died young, in the flu epidemic that followed the war, in 1919 and 1920. In 2017, a hundred years after the first appearance, Pope Francis canonized them at Fatima, two children named saints not for dying as martyrs but for how they lived. Lucia became a nun and lived until 2005. The Church judged the Fatima appearances worthy of belief in 1930, and popes have gone there on pilgrimage. But Catholic teaching calls these private revelations. They add nothing to the faith; the Church allows and encourages devotion to them, and does not require any Catholic to believe them. What Fatima asks for, though, is old: the rosary, and Mary as the one who points to her son. As she said in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "all generations shall call me blessed." On the thirteenth of May, some Catholics pray a decade for peace.
screen: `EVERY THIRTEENTH THROUGH OCTOBER.` · `PRAY, DO PENANCE, PRAY FOR PEACE.` · `TWO CHILDREN, SAINTS IN 2017.` · `WORTHY OF BELIEF, NOT REQUIRED.` · then, large: `ALL GENERATIONS SHALL CALL ME BLESSED.`

segments.voice: A decade of the rosary is one Our Father, ten Hail Marys and one Glory Be; if you pray, you can pray one now, on beads or on your fingers, for one place at war, naming the place first. If you don't pray, sit with the name of that place, and the children there, for ten slow breaths, and then a few more.
Fatima. The Portuguese village where three shepherd children said Mary appeared in 1917, asking for the rosary, penance and prayers for peace. Her day is the thirteenth of May. Today's word.
Your line: pray for peace. Ten Hail Marys, one place, one name. See you tomorrow.

669.title: The Ascension
669.hook: forty days after Easter; in many places moved to Sunday
669.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter, on a Thursday, or where bishops have transferred it, on the following Sunday; many then pray a novena to the Holy Spirit in the days before Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatima: three children and a request for the rosary in wartime. Your line was pray for peace.

An apprentice's last day goes like this. For years you've worked beside the master, watched his hands, handed him tools. Then one morning he gives you the keys, says the shop is yours, and walks out. You stand there holding the keys, staring at the door. That's roughly where the disciples are at the start of the Acts of the Apostles: forty days after Easter, on a hill outside Jerusalem, staring at the sky. Two strangers in white have a question for them.
screen: `THE KEYS TO THE SHOP.` → `FORTY DAYS AFTER EASTER.` → `STARING AT THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it twice, at the end of his Gospel and at the start of Acts. Acts says that for forty days after his passion Jesus showed himself alive and spoke of the kingdom of God. Then, on the Mount of Olives, he tells them they'll be his witnesses to the ends of the earth, and while they watch, he's lifted up and a cloud takes him out of their sight. And then the two men in white, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?" It's almost funny. Stop looking up. There's work down here. Mark's Gospel ends the same way, with the apostles going out: "But they going forth preached every where: the Lord working withal." Catholics believe the Ascension is not Jesus leaving the world, but the risen Christ, body and all, entering the glory of the Father, and from there sending the Spirit. The forty days count from Easter Sunday, so the feast falls on a Thursday, Ascension Thursday. But in many places, including much of the United States, the bishops have moved it to the following Sunday so that more people can keep it. Counted from the Thursday, nine days remain before Pentecost. Acts says the disciples went back to the upper room with Mary and the women and kept praying together, and tradition says those days of prayer gave Catholics the novena, nine days of prayer. The master has handed over the keys. The work is theirs now, and he promised not to leave them alone with it.
screen: `FORTY DAYS, THEN A CLOUD.` · `WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP?` · `THURSDAY, OR MOVED TO SUNDAY.` · `NINE DAYS OF PRAYER TO PENTECOST.` · then, large: `YE MEN OF GALILEE, WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP TO HEAVEN?`

segments.voice: Go to a window or step outside if you can, and look up for a few breaths: clouds, blue, gray, a ceiling if that's what you have. Then lower your eyes and look slowly at what's actually here, the street, the room, the people, the dishes in the sink, and ask one question: what here is mine to do? If you pray, you can ask for help with it.
The Ascension. Forty days after Easter, the risen Jesus taken up into heaven before the apostles' eyes. Kept on a Thursday, or in many places the following Sunday. Today's word.
Your line: the work is ours now. Eyes down from the sky, hands on the work. That's six hundred sixty-nine.

670.title: Pentecost
670.hook: the golden sequence: come, father of the poor
670.howItsDone: On Pentecost Sunday Catholics wear red at Mass, hear the story of the Spirit's coming in Acts 2, and sing or recite the sequence Veni, Sancte Spiritus before the Gospel; the Easter season ends that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ascension, and two men in white: why stand you looking up? Your line was the work is ours now.

The apostles are gathered in one place with Mary and some of the women, praying and waiting. Jerusalem outside is full of pilgrims for a harvest festival, the feast of weeks, fifty days after Passover. Then, Acts says, a sound from heaven like a mighty wind fills the whole house, and something appears like tongues of fire, resting on each one of them. They spill out into the street speaking, and a crowd gathered from many nations hears them, each in their own language. Centuries later, someone wrote a song for this day, and the Church still sings it before the Gospel.
screen: `TOGETHER IN ONE PLACE.` → `WIND, AND TONGUES OF FIRE.` → `A SONG FOR THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Pentecost comes from the Greek for fiftieth: fifty days after Easter, the way the Jewish feast of weeks falls fifty days after Passover. Acts describes it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "there appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire." On this day the Mass has a sequence, an old poem sung after the second reading. The Missal's instructions require a sequence on just two days: Easter, and this one. It's called the golden sequence, and it's usually credited to Stephen Langton, an archbishop of Canterbury, though nobody can prove he wrote it. It opens in Latin: "Veni, Sancte Spiritus." Come, Holy Spirit. Then a run of lines, each one calling the Spirit by a new name. The first is "Veni, pater pauperum." Come, father of the poor. Then giver of gifts, light of hearts, best comforter, the soul's sweet guest. Later verses ask the Spirit to wash what is stained, water what is dry, heal what is wounded, bend what is stiff, warm what is cold. Notice where it starts. Of all the names it could have used first, it chose the poor. Not the powerful, not the learned. In Acts, the Spirit fell on a roomful of ordinary people, fishermen among them, and a few verses later the new community is selling what it owns and dividing it, as anyone had need. The sequence remembers that, and puts the poor at the head of its list.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE FIFTIETH DAY.` · `TONGUES AS IT WERE OF FIRE.` · `THE GOLDEN SEQUENCE.` · `IT STARTS WITH THE POOR.` · then, large: `VENI, PATER PAUPERUM.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing slow and bring to mind one place in you that's dry, or cold, or stiff: a resentment, a tiredness, a door you've closed. If you pray, you can say the old opening words on your breath, in Latin or English: Veni, Sancte Spiritus, come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, breathe in as if you were opening a window in that room.
Pentecost. Greek for fiftieth: the day fifty days after Easter when tongues of fire rested on the apostles and the golden sequence calls the Spirit by many names. Today's word.
Your line: come, father of the poor. Wind, fire, and a roomful of ordinary people. Day six hundred seventy.

671.title: Trinity Sunday
671.hook: the Sunday after Pentecost is about who God is
671.howItsDone: On the Sunday after Pentecost Catholics celebrate Trinity Sunday, wearing white at Mass and professing the Creed; every day Catholics mark themselves with the sign of the cross in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost and the golden sequence, Veni Sancte Spiritus. Your line was come, father of the poor.

Christmas, Good Friday, Easter, Pentecost: each remembers something that happened, a birth, a death, a rising, a wind in a room. Trinity Sunday is different. Nothing happened on it. No event, no saint, no story. The week after Pentecost, having walked through the whole year of what God did, the Church stops and asks the question underneath all of it: who is God? A child raised Catholic is handed the answer before they have words for it, each time an adult traces a cross over them.
screen: `A FEAST WITH NO EVENT.` → `WHO IS GOD?` → `AN ANSWER TRACED ON YOUR BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's a surprise first: the word Trinity isn't in the Bible. What's there is a pattern. At the end of Matthew, the risen Jesus sends the apostles out, in the Douay-Rheims: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Notice it says the name, singular, then three. Paul ends a letter to Corinth with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost. Early Christians found themselves praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and needed words for what they were already doing. A writer in North Africa named Tertullian, arguing against a teacher called Praxeas, used the Latin trinitas, a threeness. Later, the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople gave the Creed Catholics still say on Sunday. The Church's teaching is one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks. The Church calls it a mystery, which in its language doesn't mean a puzzle to give up on. It means something true that you can keep going deeper into forever. The feast itself spread slowly through the Middle Ages, until a pope put it on the calendar of the whole Church. There's a famous story that Saint Patrick explained the Trinity with a shamrock. It's lovely, and it's a later legend; his own writings don't mention it. What Catholics actually do every day is simpler. They touch forehead, chest and both shoulders, and say the name.
screen: `THE WORD ISN'T IN THE BIBLE.` · `TERTULLIAN: TRINITAS.` · `ONE GOD, THREE PERSONS.` · `A MYSTERY TO GO DEEPER INTO.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Make the sign of the cross three times, slowly: the first at your usual speed, noticing how quickly it's over; the second pausing at each touch, forehead, chest, left shoulder, right shoulder; the third letting each name take a whole breath. If you're not someone who makes the sign, simply sit and notice your breath going in, resting, going out.
Trinity Sunday. The Sunday after Pentecost, a feast of the mystery of one God in three persons. Today's word.

672.title: Corpus Christi
672.hook: the Eucharist carried through the streets
672.howItsDone: On Corpus Christi, the Thursday after Trinity Sunday or, in many countries, the following Sunday, Catholic parishes celebrate the Eucharist and often hold a procession carrying the host in a monstrance through the streets, stopping at outdoor altars for Benediction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trinity Sunday and the sign of the cross. Your line was one god, three persons.

In towns from Spain to the Philippines to Brooklyn, on one Sunday in early summer, traffic stops. Children in first-communion white scatter rose petals on the pavement. In some places the streets have been covered overnight in carpets of colored sawdust and flowers. A priest walks under a canopy carried on four poles, holding up a gold sunburst with a small white host at its center. Behind him, a brass band, a choir, families, the elderly with walkers. They stop at little altars set up on street corners.
screen: `TRAFFIC STOPS.` → `PETALS AND SAWDUST CARPETS.` → `A GOLD SUNBURST UNDER A CANOPY.`

segments.voice: Corpus Christi is Latin for the body of Christ. Catholics believe that at Mass the bread becomes Christ's body, truly present, and they already celebrate that every Holy Thursday. But Holy Thursday is crowded with the passion. So in the 1200s a nun in Belgium, Juliana of Liège, pressed for a feast of its own, with nothing else in the way. In 1264 Pope Urban IV established it for the whole Church, and tradition says he asked Thomas Aquinas to write the prayers and hymns. Some of the best known Latin hymns come from that work: Pange lingua, with its last verses, Tantum ergo, still sung at Benediction, and the long sequence Lauda Sion. The Gospel for the feast in one year is John six, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." The gold sunburst is called a monstrance, from the Latin monstrare, to show. The whole point is showing. The host isn't kept in the tabernacle today. It's carried out of the church, past the bakery and the bus stop and the bar, through the places people actually live. Christians understand the Eucharist in different ways: some see it mainly as a memorial, while Catholics, Orthodox and a number of other churches speak of a real presence. For Catholics, today's procession says something simple: the Christ they receive at the altar belongs on the street too. And this ends week ninety-six: Divine Mercy, the Good Shepherd, Fatima, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Trinity, and now the body carried through town.
screen: `CORPUS CHRISTI: THE BODY OF CHRIST.` · `JULIANA ASKS; URBAN IV, 1264.` · `A MONSTRANCE: FOR SHOWING.` · `OUT OF THE CHURCH, INTO THE STREET.` · then, large: `I AM THE LIVING BREAD WHICH CAME DOWN FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly outside, even just to the corner and back, or picture your street from your window. Pass each door in your mind, the family with the new baby, the house that's been quiet since someone died, the shop owner, the person you've never met, and if you pray, pray for each one as you pass; if you don't, simply wish each household well.
Corpus Christi. Latin for the body of Christ: the feast of the Eucharist, established for the whole Church in 1264, kept with processions through the streets. Today's word.
